source: Steyvers et al. (2024/2025) What Large Language Models Know and What People Think They Know
finding: Users trust LLM answers more than the model's own confidence warrants. Matching the explanation's wording to the model's real confidence narrows the gap.
numbers: N=301 Prolific (+81 in Exp 3). ECE: model GPT-3.5 .104 vs human default .264 vs modified .150; PaLM2 .154/.291/.225; GPT-4o .141/.165/.111. AUC: model .751/.746/.781; human default .589/.602/.592; modified .694/.652/.689.
limits: Human judges of LLM output, not an agent judging itself. Last 9k chars unread. MMLU (350 q) and TriviaQA (336 q) only.
agent_relevance: A fluent first answer is not evidence of validity. A trust gate must use track record or calibrated confidence, never fluency.

source: Steyvers et al. (2024/2025) What Large Language Models Know and What People Think They Know (explanation length)
finding: Longer explanations raise confidence in the answer but do not help people tell right from wrong.
numbers: Long vs short explanation raised confidence (BF=25). Discrimination AUC 0.54 (long) vs 0.57 (uncertainty only), BF=.23. Self-assessed expertise did not predict calibration (BF<1).
limits: Same paper, MMLU and TriviaQA.
agent_relevance: Supports length-normalised scoring (G5) and no trust from verbosity.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false in the right format. P(True) (judge own proposed answer) improves when the model sees several of its own samples. P(IK) (predict if it knows before answering) works but generalises only partly to new tasks.
numbers: Abstract page only; no numbers extracted.
quote: larger models are well-calibrated on diverse multiple choice and true/false questions
limits: Calibration is format dependent and degrades on new tasks.
agent_relevance: A per-task-class self-knowledge signal is possible but must be validated on the class it is used for. Matches the Kahneman-Klein point that intuition is valid only in the learned environment.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: For RLHF models, verbalized confidence is better calibrated than token probabilities. Best prompt varied by dataset. Chain-of-thought did not consistently help calibration.
numbers: ECE label-prob vs best verbalized: GPT-4 TriviaQA .078 vs .024; SciQ .219 vs .028; TruthfulQA .445 vs .082. ChatGPT TriviaQA .140 vs .047; TruthfulQA .451 vs .125. Claude 2 SciQ .181 vs .048. Abstract: ECE often cut by relative 50%.
limits: 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Verbalized confidence is cheap, but see next line: low ECE does not mean good discrimination.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration (discrimination)
finding: Even when calibrated, confidence can barely separate right from wrong on adversarial or feedback-poor tasks.
numbers: AUC best-verbalized TruthfulQA: GPT-4 .632, ChatGPT .492, Claude 1 .350, Claude 2 .446. TriviaQA AUC: GPT-4 .937, Claude 2 .918.
limits: AUC taken from the same method row as the best-ECE method.
agent_relevance: On low-validity classes (TruthfulQA-like), the first answer's stated confidence is near useless. A per-class record must supplement it.

source: Michael, BenShushan, Bien, Moore (2026) Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models
finding: LLMs show the hard-easy effect like humans: overconfident on hard sets, underconfident on easy ones.
numbers: 11 models. Mean stated confidence 88% vs accuracy 79%. LifeEval hardest: 34.2% confidence vs 9.6% actual; easiest: 80.5% vs 92.0%.
limits: No human study run and no intervention tested. Summary page, not full PDF.
agent_relevance: Confidence tracks difficulty feel, not validity. Treat high confidence on hard classes as suspect.

source: Michael et al. (2026) Confidence Calibration in LLMs (reasoning vs chat models)
finding: Reasoning models are much better calibrated than chat models.
numbers: LifeEval ECE 0.037 (5 reasoning models) vs 0.150 (6 chat models). Confidence-correctness correlation .94 vs .48. Rounding to multiples of 5%: chat 91.4% vs reasoning 61.1%.
limits: Models: DeepSeek-R1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, o3, Claude Sonnet 4/3.7 vs DeepSeek-V3, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-4o, Claude Haiku 3, Llama-3.1 70B/8B.
agent_relevance: Gate quality depends on model class; re-measure per model.

source: Lacombe, Wu, Dilworth (2025) Don't Think Twice! Over-Reasoning Impairs Confidence Calibration
finding: More thinking tokens made calibration worse past a small budget.
numbers: Gemini 2.5 Flash ClimateX accuracy 41.7% (0 tokens), peak 45.0% at 64-192, 35.7% at 768, 41.7% at 24,576. Overconfidence +6% at 0 tokens to +21.3% at 384; IARC +15.6% to +35.6% at 320. ClimateX 8,094 statements (300 test); IARC 1,053.
limits: Workshop paper; one narrow task type; one model family for the budget curve.
agent_relevance: Deliberation does not repair an invalid intuition. Adding thinking length is not a trust signal.

source: Lacombe et al. (2025) Don't Think Twice (search vs reasoning)
finding: Giving the model search evidence beat pure reasoning by a wide margin. Bigger was not better calibrated.
numbers: Gemini 2.5 Pro with Search 89.3% (kappa 85.7%) vs 48.7% pure reasoning; Flash with Search 88.3%. RoBERTa-Large fine-tuned 53.7%, GPT-4o 44.0%, non-expert humans 36.2%. Llama-3-8B-Chat beat Llama-3-70B-Chat.
limits: Knowledge-intensive IPCC/IARC statements.
agent_relevance: When the class lacks validity because information is missing, route to evidence, not more reasoning.

source: Sprague et al. (2024) To CoT or not to CoT?
finding: Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic tasks. On MMLU direct answering matches CoT unless the question or response contains an equals sign.
numbers: Meta-analysis of 100+ papers plus own evaluation on 20 datasets, 14 models. Abstract page only.
limits: No per-task numbers read.
agent_relevance: Task class is the unit of trust: for non-symbolic classes the fast answer is as good, so skip deliberation.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind Your Step (by Step) (implicit learning)
finding: On tasks where verbal deliberation hurts humans, CoT hurts models. Implicit pattern learning is worse with step-by-step reasoning.
numbers: Artificial grammar, absolute drop with CoT: o1-preview 36.3% (vs GPT-4o zero-shot), GPT-4o 23.1%, Claude 3 Opus 8.0%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet -1.8%, Gemini 1.5 Pro 6.05%, Llama 3.1 70B 8.8%, Llama 3.1 8B 1.98%.
quote: Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse
limits: o1 comparison is not matched (o1 cannot turn reasoning off). 100k of 144k chars read.
agent_relevance: Rare machine counterpart to the valid-intuition boundary: for recognition-type classes, deliberation can degrade. Supports G1.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind Your Step (face recognition, exceptions)
finding: CoT also hurts face recognition and makes rule-with-exceptions learning slower.
numbers: Face recognition drop: GPT-4o 12.8%, Claude 3 Opus 14.4%, Gemini 1.5 Pro 11.4%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 3.0%, InternVL2-76B 2.0% (p=0.44, not significant). Rounds to learn exceptions: GPT-4o 2.9 to 12.5 (+331%), Claude 3.5 Sonnet 2.3 to 6.4, Claude 3 Opus 2.4 to 5.5.
limits: Three of six tasks read; others mixed.
agent_relevance: Same as above; effect size varies a lot by model, so test per model.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2022/2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: GPT-3 shows human-like intuitive errors on CRT and semantic illusions. ChatGPT and GPT-4 avoid them and act hyper-rational.
numbers: Abstract page only; no scores read.
limits: Change attributed to capability; not tied to validity conditions.
agent_relevance: The intuition error profile shifts across model generations, so any trust gate must be re-fitted per model version.

source: Ziabari et al. (2025) Reasoning on a Spectrum (S1 vs S2 models)
finding: Models aligned to intuitive (S1) vs analytic (S2) answers each win on different task classes.
numbers: 2,000 questions from 10 heuristics; 13 benchmarks; Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B. Llama exact match S2 DPO vs base: AddSub 89.87 vs 82.47, SingleEq 94.37 vs 90.72, AQuA SimPO 54.72 vs 48.82. S1 better on commonsense: CSQA 72.81 vs 71.42, PIQA 83.94 vs 83.16. S2 worse on StrategyQA 60.87 vs 67.55.
limits: Needs fine-tuning; small 7-8B models; last 23k chars unread.
agent_relevance: The arithmetic vs commonsense split matches the validity framing: intuition is fine for knowledge retrieval, not for computation.

source: Ziabari et al. (2025) Reasoning on a Spectrum (entropy mixing)
finding: A training-free mixer picks S1 or S2 output by token entropy and beats the base model on most benchmarks.
numbers: Best weight w=0.4. Llama DPO-dynamic beats base on 12 of 13, SimPO 11 of 13. Mistral DPO 11 of 13, SimPO 12 of 13.
limits: Needs token probabilities and the two aligned models.
agent_relevance: A cheap confidence gate based on entropy. Only usable with logprob access.

source: DynamicMind (2025) A Tri-Mode Thinking System for LLMs
finding: A small router (DeBERTaV3-base) picks fast, normal or slow mode per question. No single mode wins everywhere.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B. Llama with router: CommonsenseQA 63.91%, MMLU 52.48%, ScienceQA 70.36%; avg thinking density 1.33 vs CoT 0.27. 80.52% of GSM8K samples best served by normal mode.
limits: Router trained on the model's own results; fast mode fails on math.
agent_relevance: A learned task-class trust gate; works as a proof of concept.

source: DynamicMind (2025) router transfer and mode shares
finding: A router trained for one LLM lost accuracy on another. Only a small fraction of items need slow mode.
numbers: Slow mode gave accuracy gains on 3.11% of items (+53.84% on those, +277.30 tokens). Normal over fast gained on 14.13% of items (+49.95%). Fast matched normal on 6% of items, saving 120.52 tokens. Removing normal mode raised tokens a lot (Llama) or cut accuracy (Qwen).
limits: Appendix case statistics, k=3 samples.
agent_relevance: The track record is model specific. Rebuild it when the model changes.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Think How to Think (TH2T)
finding: Teaching reasoning models to judge difficulty cuts length with no accuracy loss on easy tasks.
limits: Needs LoRA training; the over-70% headline holds only for 7B.
agent_relevance: Easy items need little deliberation, but the hardest class lost accuracy. Keep the gate conservative on high-stakes items.

source: Chen et al. (2024/2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=?
finding: o1-like models spend lots of compute on trivial problems. A self-training method cuts overthinking while keeping accuracy on GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME.
numbers: Abstract page only; no numbers read.
limits: Numbers not verified this session.
agent_relevance: Documents the cost of always deliberating.

source: Yue et al. (2023/2024) LLM Cascades with Mixture of Thoughts
finding: A cheap model answers first. If its sampled answers disagree, escalate to GPT-4. Disagreement signals difficulty.
numbers: Six benchmarks. Performance comparable to GPT-4 alone at about 40% of its cost. Abstract page only.
limits: Agreement from one model is correlated (G4): a hint, not proof.
agent_relevance: The closest LLM implementation of 'trust the first answer unless a signal says otherwise' (G1).

source: Kim et al. (2026) ReASC
finding: Stage 1 accepts a single response if its confidence passes a calibrated threshold. Only the rest get more samples.
numbers: GSM8K Gemma-3-4B: SC k=16 92.12% at 32.67 TF; ReASC 92.04% at 9.45 TF (-71.1%). Qwen-2.5-7B 94.31 vs 94.09, -74.9%. Gemma-3-27B 97.04 vs 96.89, -82.4%. Stage 1 accepted 51.18% at 97.78% accuracy (offline), 33.28% at 98.41% (online).
limits: Mostly math; thresholds fitted on labeled validation data or by Gaussian mixture.
agent_relevance: Concrete recipe: single-answer acceptance with a threshold fitted on a validation record. About half of items accepted at about 98% accuracy.

source: Aghazadeh et al. (2025) CGES
finding: Bayesian posterior over candidate answers from per-sample confidence. Stop sampling when the top answer passes a threshold.
numbers: Five benchmarks, 3 seeds: 4.90 calls vs 16.00 (-69.4%), accuracy 73.55 vs 73.61. GPQA with MARS 3.61 calls, 52.69 vs 51.01. MMLU_Pro 6.77 calls, +0.02. Reward-model reference 5.27 calls, 73.42%.
limits: Workshop paper; 7B models; small dips on easy MATH500/GSM8K for token-prob variants.
agent_relevance: A confidence-driven stopping rule that code can count (G5).

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: A retrieval LM forecaster approaches but does not beat the human crowd. It matches the crowd where the crowd is uncertain. Combining both is best.
numbers: 914 test questions. Brier: system .179 (71.5% acc), crowd .149 (77.0%), weighted aggregate .146 (77.8%); random .250; best zero-shot GPT-4 .208. Crowd uncertain (.3-.7): system .238 vs crowd .240. 5+ relevant articles: .175 vs .142. Calibration RMS .42 vs .38. Fine-tuning .186 to .179.
limits: Standard errors assume i.i.d. but data are time series. 100k chars read. Recalibration did not help.
agent_relevance: In low-validity domains no first answer is trustworthy. Combine mechanically with an outside view. Echoes Meehl.

source: Copus (2025/2026, forthcoming) Computational Clinical Judgment: Predicting Risk with LLMs
finding: LLMs read parole transcripts and predict rearrest. GPT-5 beat a 91-variable actuarial ML baseline and added signal it missed. Its stated reasons did not explain its predictions.
numbers: 7 LLMs, 113 transcripts; baseline trained on 4,000 cases with 91 variables. A search snippet of another version says p=0.007 with 6 LLMs and 141 transcripts: versions disagree.
limits: Abstract only; unreviewed; versions differ.
agent_relevance: A first Meehl-style LLM vs actuarial test. Unfaithful reasons argue against trusting self-explanations (G2).

source: Scholten, Rebholz, Hutter (2024/2026) Metacognitive Myopia in Large Language Models
finding: Theory: LLMs lack monitoring and control. Five symptoms include base-rate neglect, using redundant information, and frequency-based decisions.
numbers: No empirical numbers (framework paper).
limits: Theoretical.
agent_relevance: Base-rate neglect is what actuarial methods fix. Suggests a code-side monitor of the first answer.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias
finding: Cognitive biases are linear directions in activations. Prompt-level debiasing helps response biases but backfires for judgment biases.
numbers: Activation steering cuts bias score 26-32%. Qwen loses up to 19.0 points on Judgment benchmarks; Llama negligible loss. 3 LLMs, 4 bias families, 25 capability benchmarks.
limits: Abstract only; open-weights; steering is not scaffold-only.
agent_relevance: A generic 'be careful' prompt can worsen judgment biases, which supports G1: use code-side checks, not blanket doubt prompts.

source: Kahneman, Sibony, Sunstein (2021) Noise (secondary summaries)
finding: Judgments on identical cases vary between people and within one person across occasions. Rules and algorithms are noise-free; decomposing and delaying intuition reduce noise.
numbers: Not opened; search snippets only.
limits: Secondary summaries; no LLM study found on repeated-case noise.
agent_relevance: Sampling gives within-model noise by design; consistency checks are the analog. Test before relying.

source: Scaling with Confidence (CAS, 2026) calibrated verbalized confidence for adaptive test-time scaling
finding: Argues frequency and entropy signals are often uncalibrated; uses calibrated verbalized confidence in the stopping criterion, checked per batch.
numbers: Not opened; snippet only.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Another stopping-rule family; verify before use.

source: DeepConf (2025) Deep Think with Confidence
finding: Uses model-internal confidence to filter low-quality reasoning traces during or after generation.
numbers: Not opened; Medium summary only.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Needs logprob access, which a scaffold using an API may lack.
